Shen Yen-li blinked and looked again at Shen Weici — at her lightly flushed cheeks, and her eyes lifting toward him, soft and unhurried.

Someone else spoke up: "Let's just go with Second Elder Sister's version — more of a challenge makes it more fun. We're all playing together; what matters is to participate."

Shen Yen-li let the matter drop, and asked a maidservant to bring out the bamboo drawing-sticks. He glanced at Song Zhang beside him, wanting to invite him in, but not quite daring.

Song Zhang looked at Shen Yen-li: "Play without me."

Shen Yen-li relaxed with relief.

Everyone drew a stick. Shen Weici looked at hers — she had drawn last.

Shen Zhao-zhao went first. With only half a sandglass of time to compose a matching couplet on the spot, it was genuinely challenging.

Most people managed by borrowing a line from older poetry and reworking the meter.

After two rounds, when it was Shen Yen-li's turn, he could not think of anything and took his penalty cup himself.

When it came to Shen Weici, she thought briefly and then said: "One night's rain falls without measure, and by morning shows no sign of yielding."

The others stared, surprised. No one had expected Shen Weici to come up with something so quickly.

Shen Zhao-zhao was irritated. She had been praised by the clan's teachers since childhood, and her poetry was considered the best in the household. No one else here could produce something so quickly — not even she could always manage it on the first try.

She quickly thought up her own line, but her eyes stayed fixed on Shen Weici.

In the next round, Fifth Young Miss was too young and naturally could not manage; Fourth Young Miss barely scraped through; Shen Si-wen produced something at the very last moment; Shen Yen-li simply gave up.

Shen Weici looked out at the rainy view and without much thought spoke: "Moss creeps over crumbling walls as autumn deepens; grass swallows broken ramparts, rain swallows more."

This verse carried a desolate, wistful feeling — like a place left by all who mattered, its warmth gone with them.

Every person in the room turned to look at Shen Weici. None of them could quite reconcile what they were seeing — a girl from the countryside who apparently had more feeling for poetry than any of them.

Song Zhang's eyes settled on Shen Weici's face — her cheeks flushed a vivid peach-pink, her inherently alluring face looking, in this moment, as though it might dissolve into the rain.

Those eyes, half-lowered and gleaming with warmth in the sound of the rain, and the line of poetry that came from those cherry-red lips — Song Zhang's gaze was almost unable to look away.

Seeing Shen Weici come through again, Shen Zhao-zhao's composure finally cracked. The sandglass was nearly run out, everyone was watching her — and she only barely produced a line in the final moment.

Shen Weici had already taken note of the look on Shen Zhao-zhao's face. In this round, no one else could answer, and it was Shen Weici's turn.

Yuedeng, seated nearby, was quietly thrilled, waiting for her young miss to shine.

She knew her young miss would certainly find an answer. The young miss had the best ear for rhyme and meter — the teacher at the village school had praised her again and again, saying she had the mind of a scholar who could sit the imperial examinations and earn a degree.

Besides, the young miss had just whispered a line to her ear not long ago: "Rain pounds all night and rushes headlong into dawn; from all four mountains, clouded air presses toward the autumn cold." She had been teaching Yuedeng to recognize the rhyme scheme — it was already composed.

But to Yuedeng's surprise, she watched the young miss furrow her brows as if thinking very hard, her eyes fixed on the sandglass, and not produce a single word until the very last grain had fallen.

chapters.title: Hidden Gems
chapters.content:
Shen Weici scrunched her brows gently, as though deep in genuine thought, her eyes fixed on the sandglass — and at the very last moment said softly: "I can't think of anything. Second Elder Sister is far better than me at this. I'll take my penalty willingly."

With that, Shen Weici took the cup from the maidservant's hand and drank all three cups of warm wine.

Shen Zhao-zhao had been on the verge of failing herself in the next round — and if she, a proper well-bred daughter of the Marquis household, had lost to Shen Weici, the humiliation would have been unbearable.

It was lucky that, even though Shen Weici had surprised her somewhat, it had only come to this.

The smile she wore turned superior. She cast Shen Weici a condescending look: "Third Younger Sister actually held her own for this many rounds — that's not bad at all."

Fourth Young Miss Shen Mingqiu said with a smile: "Even so, Third Elder Sister was impressive — I didn't expect it at all."

Shen Mingqiu genuinely felt a new respect for Shen Weici. The time they had played the dice-board game before — somehow Shen Weici had drawn with Shen Zhao-zhao, which was remarkable in itself, since a draw at dice was rare. She had already found that astonishing.

Shen Weici smiled warmly: "I was only muddling through by luck. I can't really claim credit for it."

"Fourth Younger Sister and Fifth Younger Sister, if they truly applied themselves, would surpass me without difficulty."

Shen Si-wen looked at Shen Weici: "Third Younger Cousin, you really are full of surprises. Did you study before?"

Shen Weici's eyes still held their quiet warmth: "I picked up a few things, but only barely scratched the surface."

"Honestly, I can't compare to Eldest Cousin or any of the sisters here."

As she spoke she rose from her chair and excused herself: "It looks as though the rain isn't going to let up. My courtyard is a little out of the way — I'll head back first."

She had just lifted her foot when Shen Zhao-zhao reached out and caught her: "Third Younger Sister, you've only played one round and you're leaving? Where's the fun in that? Surely Third Younger Sister should stay for at least three rounds."

Shen Zhao-zhao had had no intention of making trouble for Shen Weici. But when Shen Weici had shown herself more capable, and everyone had praised her for it — even the people who hadn't particularly liked her before — Shen Zhao-zhao couldn't stomach it. She had to do something.

Shen Weici paused and looked down at Shen Zhao-zhao seated in her chair — her eyes full of contemptuous disdain, with a flicker of something malicious underneath, as if Shen Weici's discomfiture brought her satisfaction.

Shen Weici had no desire for conflict with Shen Zhao-zhao. They were both of the Second Branch; any clash between them would only hurt her own position.

But perhaps it was the wine working through her now — that fruit wine that seemed so mild was beginning to have its effect, making her body warm and her head faintly light.

She smiled: "The sky looks as though it's nearly dark — if Second Elder Sister wants to play on, how about I come over tomorrow and keep you company?"

Shen Zhao-zhao gave her a look: "It's still quite bright out. Perhaps it'll be over quickly. Why not stay a little longer?"

She turned to Shen Si-wen and Shen Yen-li: "Don't you both agree?"

Both of them shrugged: "Either way works for us — nothing interesting to go back to anyway."

Shen Mingqiu knew how to read a room, and smiled agreeably: "Fifth Younger Sister and I are fine with it too."

Shen Weici closed her eyes a moment and conceded.

For the next two rounds — 'wind' and 'leaf' in turn — Shen Weici still let herself lose in the final round, when only she and Shen Zhao-zhao remained. She simply didn't want to drink the full three cups, and she didn't want to draw Shen Zhao-zhao's real resentment.

Shen Weici could hardly drink any more, so after losing she only drank the first cup and quietly poured the other two into her sleeve.

Shen Zhao-zhao's expression of triumph grew more pleased, and even her temper warmed during conversation.

When they were about to begin the next round, a maidservant came hurrying up the stairs from below. She glanced around the room, greeted the ladies, and then quickly made her way to Shen Weici's side and leaned in: "Third Miss, Master Zhang is here."

The maidservant's voice was very low, and the sound of rain and the chatter of everyone else covered it — no one else heard.

But Song Zhang, who had been lounging listlessly against the railing watching the rain, turned his head back and let his gaze settle on Shen Weici.

He watched her turn slightly, her wide sleeve resting decorously in her lap, her back presented to the room. Her posture was elegant, and in the quiet depths of her eyes something swirled — a feeling he could not quite read.

Then he saw her rise and step to a corner of the room, her back to everyone, leaving only a willowy dark-blue silhouette.

He looked away without interest.

Shen Weici asked the maidservant in a low voice: "Where is he now? Is he with my Father?"

The maidservant shook her head: "Master Zhang has just come from the Second Master's quarters. He is now waiting at the gate of the young miss's courtyard."

"I asked him to come inside and sit in the hall, but he said since you were not there, it wouldn't be proper to go in. He said he would wait outside until you returned."

Shen Weici heard this and nodded. She told the maidservant to go back, and added a reminder that the wind outside was cold and the rain was heavy — please bring him a cup of hot tea to warm him up.

The girl quietly acknowledged this and hurried off.

Shen Weici turned back and, seeing everyone's eyes on her, went over and said quietly: "Something has come up with a maidservant back in my courtyard. I need to go see to it. I'll join everyone again next time."

Someone asked: "What happened to the maidservant?"

Shen Weici smiled: "Only a small thing — a quarrel of sorts. I'll go and look into it."

Shen Zhao-zhao looked at Shen Weici: "And you have to manage something so trivial yourself?"

"Or is it that you can't bear to lose?"

That remark was a dig about the dice game — Shen Zhao-zhao had been nursing that grievance, and saying it aloud now finally gave her some relief.

Shen Weici looked at Shen Zhao-zhao, her eyes still quiet and serene: "I truly am no match for Second Elder Sister. But there is indeed something in the courtyard, and I did not mean to ruin everyone's mood. I'll come and make it up to Second Elder Sister another time."

Shen Zhao-zhao, seeing Shen Weici make herself small before her, felt her air of superiority deepen, and waved her off impatiently: "Go then, go."

Shen Weici gathered her sleeves and walked toward the stairs.

Song Zhang looked down from the window above. Before long, on the stone bridge below, Shen Weici appeared — a pale umbrella in hand, a white cloak around her shoulders, moving along the curved path with slow, careful steps. She passed through a blur of banana leaves and was gone.

From behind him, a murmur: "Third Younger Sister really is lovely — and such a gentle temper too. I think her breeding and bearing are not behind any well-born young lady. She might well make a fine match one day."

Shen Si-wen turned to look at Shen Zhao-zhao: "I hear Third Younger Cousin has come of age. Second Aunt, has she begun looking for a match?"

Shen Zhao-zhao's smile was cold: "She may have a pretty face — but she's still dragging around country habits underneath it. What good family would want her?"

"They'll find her any old match here in the capital and she should consider herself lucky. It'll be better than anything she would've found in Yuyang — she ought to be grateful."

Song Zhang looked at the empty distance where the figure had long since disappeared, then stood from his place against the railing and walked out with long strides.

Shen Zhao-zhao saw Song Zhang leave without so much as a word of farewell and wanted to call after him, but stopped herself.

Song Zhang did as he pleased. No one dared question it. From the start he had almost never stayed in this estate, and today had been the rare occasion he had come and eaten with them — though not for very long.

Shen Mingqiu watched Song Zhang's retreating back disappear and said to the others: "Song Elder Brother must be almost twenty-two now — do you think they're looking for a match for him?"

Shen Si-wen shook his head: "Second Elder Brother is a cold one. He's only been back in the capital a little over a year, and already no shortage of women have thrown themselves at him. Probably Aunty is looking into it."

"Apparently a few days ago some woman deliberately stepped in front of his carriage just to get his attention."

Shen Mingqiu asked curiously: "And then what happened?"

Shen Si-wen clicked his tongue: "Then Second Elder Brother had the carriage drive straight over her. They say she'll never walk right again."

Everyone in the room drew a sharp breath.

chapters.title: A Solemn Intention
chapters.content:
Before Shen Weici had even reached the gate of her courtyard, she spotted the dark green of Zhang Yuanheng's robe from a distance — a tall, upright figure standing under the eave of the gate, straight as a pine.

In the rain and mist, white threads of water vapor rose around everything, blurring the world into pale vagueness. But that figure grew clearer by degrees as she approached, and she could feel, even from this distance, the weight of his eyes on her.

She lowered her lashes, lifted her skirt, and walked up to stand before him.

"Why didn't Master Zhang come inside to sit?"

Zhang Yuanheng's gaze remained fixed on her, taking in her cool yet gentle expression: "Third Miss is still living under her family's roof. For me to go inside — it would violate propriety, and I feared it might invite people to talk."

Shen Weici smiled faintly and looked up at him: "Master Zhang has already seen my Father, I take it?"

Zhang Yuanheng smiled back: "I saw Minister Shen first. It was actually someone from his quarters who brought me here."

Shen Weici glanced at the young manservant standing nearby — one of her father's most reliable attendants from the study. That was reassuring. No one could say anything untoward.

The tall figure of Zhang Yuanheng before her radiated a quiet warmth. Three steps separated them, and yet Shen Weici felt, at that moment, inexplicably at ease.

She asked again: "Did Master Zhang come with something to say?"

Zhang Yuanheng looked into the eyes looking up at him — misty, like the rain itself. His own cheeks grew warm, and he felt like a young boy struck by his first feeling — slightly at a loss for words in front of a fifteen-year-old girl.

He smiled inwardly at himself, and held out the small box he had been carrying: "What Third Miss said the other day — I went home and thought about it carefully. I also consulted my father. He has agreed."

"I came today specifically to see Third Miss, hoping to make my intentions more evident — so Third Miss will know I am not a man who speaks carelessly. Having made a promise, I wished to make it in person, and let Third Miss be at ease."

In truth, when Zhang Yuanheng had been waiting at the courtyard gate, he had looked over the whole courtyard. The position of the place was clearly out of the way — and the courtyard itself was old, lichen creeping along the walls, the pillars faded and unrepaired, the courtyard bricks crumbling underfoot. He could scarcely believe that a household as grand as this Marquis estate could arrange quarters like this for a young lady.

He had met Minister Shen twice now, and the man had spoken of Shen Weici as a daughter he cherished. Yet if he truly cherished her — why was she placed here?

He looked at Shen Weici, and his heart only grew more earnest. She had endured all of this, yet remained gentle and quiet through it all, the only sign of inner sorrow a faint shadow deep in her eyes — no complaints, no grievances on display. He was deeply drawn to her, and wanted to do all that he could for her.

The sound of Zhang Yuanheng's voice came to her again: "Everything else I have to say is written in the letter inside. Please accept it, Third Miss."

The box in her hands still held the faint warmth of his. She tightened her fingers around it, then looked up at him: "I will go home and read it carefully."

Zhang Yuanheng smiled, and then he noticed it — the pink flush on Shen Weici's porcelain cheeks and the delicate trace of fruit wine on her breath. That soft, warm fragrance mingled with her own, and his throat moved. Without quite meaning to, his body leaned an inch closer. His gaze lingered on the lowered lashes of her eyes.

The lashes were very long, and when he looked more closely, the tip of her nose seemed to carry a slight sheen of moisture — as if mist had settled and left its trace.

His heart beat faster. He knew he ought to go. But his body did not want to leave.

He asked quietly: "Third Miss has been drinking fruit wine?"

Shen Weici felt him lean slightly toward her, though it was only by a fraction — not enough to make her feel he was overstepping.

She did not step back. She nodded and said softly: "I drank a few sips of warm wine just now at the pavilion."

Zhang Yuanheng also nodded, looking at her. She clearly could not hold her drink well — the outer corners of her eyes were tinged pink.

The slight upward tilt at those outer corners, the long lashes beneath them, the smoothness of her jaw — white, impossibly white.

He knew he had no reason to keep her talking. The rain was heavy, and he was worried about her frail constitution — that she might take in the cold if she stood out here too long. Pressing down the reluctance rising in his chest, he said: "The rain is cold, Third Miss. Please go back inside."

Shen Weici looked at Zhang Yuanheng. He was standing in front of her, beneath the eave, and she saw that he had been shielding her from a good portion of the rain blowing in. His sleeve was damp, and small droplets of rain clung to his hair.

Her heart moved. She looked at him again, and the warmth in his eyes was unmistakably genuine. He had surely noticed the state of her courtyard, too — and yet here he was, unchanged. That comforted her more than she expected.

It smoothed over the last trace of uneasy doubt she had been carrying.

She wanted to find a steady, reliable companion. She hoped Zhang Yuanheng would be that person — someone to whom she could give her trust, slowly and by degrees. Someone for whom she would bear children and keep a peaceful home.

There were a thousand things she could not put into words. She knew she would never be able to give herself entirely — that deep in her heart she would always keep a path back, something held in reserve, so that no matter how things ended, she might still find a way out.

She nodded, and said softly: "The road is slippery, Master Zhang — please take care on your way."

Zhang Yuanheng nodded, then looked at Shen Weici one last, long time. He took the umbrella his attendant held out, opened it, and walked into the rain.

But he had only gone two steps when he stopped and turned back, unable to help himself. Shen Weici was still standing under the eave, watching him go. Her eyes still held that cool, clear quality — but now, when he looked at them, he thought he could detect a thread of warmth.

She stood in her fine garments, dark hair loosely pinned, a few loose strands stirring in the wind — sweeping across her delicate shoulder, then gently across her cheek. And behind her, the sparse and quiet courtyard seemed at once out of place with her and perfectly matched — just like the faint melancholy in the depths of her eyes.

She was warm, yet somehow also cold.

He said quietly: "Third Miss, please go back. You needn't see me off."

Shen Weici smiled: "I will wait until Master Zhang has gone first."

Those words warmed Zhang Yuanheng's heart. The lingering, uncertain feeling that had unsettled him only moments before dissolved entirely. He smiled and, not wanting to make her stand outside any longer, finally turned away.

When Zhang Yuanheng's figure had faded into the distance, Shen Weici lowered her eyes to the box in her hands, and made to turn back inside.

Her head was swimming badly, and the wind sent a fresh ache through it. The fruit wine was catching up to her, and she felt a wave of exhaustion. She was thinking of lying down for a while.

But just as she turned, the corner of her eye caught a flash of red — Song Zhang, in a scarlet robe, passing by with a black umbrella. He looked as though he was simply walking past, as though by chance — and yet stopped exactly in front of her courtyard gate.

Shen Weici paused and looked at Song Zhang, standing there in the rain.

He still wore the black-and-gold sword at his hip, a gold crown binding his hair, two daggers thrust through his waistband, jade pendants at his belt, and gold thread glinting in the pattern of his robe — an aura of cold, imposing authority that pressed down simply by standing there.

chapters.title: He Had Underestimated Her
chapters.content:
Rain streamed from the eaves like a curtain, a transparent net hanging between the two of them.

Shen Weici said nothing. She waited for Song Zhang to speak.

He looked as though he had come to say something. She had already turned it over in her mind several times.

Song Zhang studied Shen Weici for a moment — his detached, indifferent gaze moving over the box in her hand, then settling on the flush of color in her cheeks.

That soft pink was vivid against her skin, carrying a faint, diffused warmth. He had just watched her stand beside Zhang Yuanheng like a small bird nestling close, head tilted, a shy blush coloring her face — a glimpse of spring warmth.

For some reason, Song Zhang found that image inexplicably irritating. He gave Shen Weici a contemptuous, mocking look — and walked on without a word.

He had thought her somewhat different from other women. But she was simply another woman trying to climb higher in the world. She had barely been in the household a month, and had already managed to catch herself a man.

He had watched clearly just now — she had stood at the courtyard gate, gazing after Zhang Yuanheng with undisguised tenderness, until she had thoroughly bewitched him.

Zhang Yuanheng was normally the most self-controlled and principled man the Emperor had around him — upright, never fawning, never demeaning himself. Even the Emperor had spoken well of him. And yet just now, in front of Shen Weici, the man had been dazed with infatuation, his soul apparently stolen clean away.

Song Zhang thought he had truly underestimated Shen Weici. He was not sure what arts of beauty she practiced.

Shen Weici noticed Song Zhang's gaze returning, again and again, to the object in her hand — that mocking contempt in his eyes impossible to miss.

He had seen what had happened just now between her and Zhang Yuanheng. He had probably drawn the worst possible conclusion.

But Shen Weici believed her own conduct had been proper. Her father's attendant had been present the whole time — nothing that happened could be considered improper. If Song Zhang wanted to make something of it, that was his own distorted thinking. She herself was here to find a suitable husband, after all.

Zhang Yuanheng had feelings for her, and she did for him as well.

That was nothing shameful.

With that thought settled, Shen Weici no longer looked at Song Zhang, and turned back into her courtyard.

Back inside, the hem of her skirt was entirely wet, and she had stood out in the rain for a good while. The cold was seeping through her again.

Yuedeng brought fresh clothes and helped her change. Shen Weici put them on, went to recline on the daybed, pulled a light quilt over herself, and only then opened Zhang Yuanheng's box.

The box was not large, but far more delicately crafted than the previous one.

She unfastened the silver clasp. On top was a letter.

Shen Weici lowered her eyes and unfolded the paper. Zhang Yuanheng had written his commitment in solemn terms, and promised to arrange for the formal proposal to be made before the new year if possible — and no later than shortly after.

At the end, she came upon a few lines of restrained feeling. Her slender fingers traced over those characters, and Zhang Yuanheng's warm, composed eyes rose up in her mind.

He was like a gentleman who kept perfect command of himself. Even in writing that he could not sleep for thinking of her, he immediately followed it with a note that he hoped she would forgive him for being too forward.

Shen Weici turned it over. She remembered that Zhang Yuanheng must be twenty-four — quite a bit older than she was. Yet this careful, tentative tenderness moved her nonetheless.

She folded the letter neatly and asked Yuedeng to put it away with the earlier ones.

Then she looked at what lay resting quietly inside the box — a jade pendant and a pair of earrings — and lifted them up to examine them.

The white jade pendant had not a single flaw. Zhang Yuanheng had written that this piece of jade had been given by his father to his mother in earlier years. When he heard that Zhang Yuanheng had someone in his heart, his father had taken out this matched set as a token of sincerity.

The jade pendant dangled from a red cord before her eyes. She sat with her head tilted slightly, gazing at it in the candlelight, her head still aching and swimming. She wanted to look at it a little longer.

Yuedeng beside her was equally transfixed: "Is this from Master Zhang? It's beautiful."

Shen Weici looked at the jade in silence for a long moment, then smiled.

Finally she looked at the pair of smoky-green jadeite earrings. Zhang Yuanheng had written that he came across them by chance and felt they would suit her, so he had bought them for her.

The earrings were neither too large nor too small, and in the lamplight the smoky color was both luminous and lovely. Even Yuedeng stared at them in a daze.

Shen Weici looked at them for a good while before asking Chuntao to put both the jade pendant and the box away together in a safe place.

She curled herself up on the bed, tired to the bone, and coughed twice. Outside it was raining and cold, and her body had begun to protest.

Yuedeng put everything away, then crouched down beside Shen Weici again: "Why does it feel even colder here in the winter?"

"The rain has made it worse. Is your knee all right, miss? I'll go heat some water over the brazier outside and fill the warming stone."

She rose to see to it.

The room was quiet, only Shen Weici left inside. The carved screen separated the inner chamber from the outer. She propped her head on her hand, dizzy, and thought to herself that she clearly could not drink — fruit wine was just as intoxicating as any other.

She had been utterly exhausted and ready to fall asleep, yet the aching in her knee kept nagging at her. She placed her palm over it, and the cold seemed to pull away every last shred of warmth her hand had left.

By the time Chuntao came in with the warming stone, Shen Weici had fallen asleep against the daybed.

Chuntao moved with the quietest possible steps, slid the warming stone in, helped Shen Weici out of her outer robe, tucked the quilt around her properly, and then tiptoed back out.

Meanwhile, Song Zhang had walked some distance past Shen Weici's courtyard before abruptly turning on his heel — only to find the gate standing empty, no one there.

He was reminded of the fact that when he heard Zhang Yuanheng was coming, he had somehow followed along this whole stretch of path for no clear reason. What did it matter to him whom Shen Weici saw?

If he kept on this path, he would either reach the rear side gate or end up in the back garden.

The attendant behind him dared not speak, but then Song Zhang's sharp gaze cut toward him: "Your master has walked the wrong way and you can't even say so?"

Minhe, who served this ancestor of a master with his life constantly at stake, dropped to one knee immediately: "It is this one's failure. I deserve the General's punishment."

Song Zhang gave a cold snort, turned with a sweep of his sleeve, and reversed his steps back toward the East Courtyard.

Minhe let out a quiet breath of relief and followed, carefully and cautiously.

Song Zhang returned to his courtyard. He had barely stepped inside the gate when he found a small, delicate maidservant waiting beneath the covered walkway outside the main room.

She had red lips and white teeth, eyes like clear autumn water — vivid and beautiful, with a high, full figure and a slender waist. The moment she saw him walk in, she came toward him like water flowing over stone.

Song Zhang had been around more women than he could count. In the capital — the pleasure houses, the flower boats — there was scarcely a place that did not know him. Women throwing themselves at him were countless. But no one in his own courtyard had ever been so bold.

He flung the umbrella to a waiting servant and stared at the maidservant with a blank, emotionless face, fingers closing around her chin: "Who sent you?"

The girl was terrified by his expression and stumbled out her answer: "It... it was the Commandery Princess who sent me."

"She said the Second Young Master had no one to warm his bed, and asked me to come and attend to the Second Young Master properly."

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow. His expression remained cold. He released his grip and stepped into the room.

He settled back into the rosewood chair, resting one hand on the armrest. He accepted the hot tea a servant brought and, looking at the maidservant who had followed him inside, let an icy, faint contempt settle into his gaze.

His dark eyes gave nothing away: "And how do you plan to attend to me?"

The maidservant's cheeks flushed crimson. She gave him a long, inviting look, and then knelt on the floor and began to crawl toward him.

Her soft body moved with practiced undulation, her slender white hands settling on Song Zhang's thigh. She glanced up at him with a shy look, then bent her head and ducked beneath his outer robe.

Song Zhang looked down, and let out a scoffing sound: "Interesting."

His mother had certainly gone to some effort.

The other maidservants in the room did not dare look. They immediately averted their eyes, retreating to the corners — but in the next moment, they all heard a sharp cry of pain.

chapters.title: The Anger He Directed at Her
chapters.content:
By now the sky had grown faintly dark. Song Zhang sat with one leg crossed over the other, the raised toe of his boot tapping steadily against the chin of the maidservant kneeling and trembling on the floor.

His black satin boot knocked at her once, then again — smearing its sole's dust across what had been a smooth, pretty face.

His voice was languid, low: "You came to attend to me, and this is all you're capable of?"

"When you go back to my mother, you'll know what to tell her?"

The maidservant immediately dropped into a series of rapid, desperate bows: "This servant knows, knows exactly what to say — please spare this servant's life, Second Young Master."

Song Zhang's earlier kick had driven straight into her solar plexus, sending blood surging to her throat. She had thought for an instant she would be killed on the spot — she was certainly not going to try that again with this man.

The Commandery Princess had sent her here to find out whether the Second Young Master was incapable. But she had just seen for herself that there was nothing incapable about him — she simply was not up to the task.

Song Zhang looked at the maidservant kowtowing on the floor, found the rhythmic knocking sound irritating, and sent her out with another kick to the shoulder.

Song Zhang had always had a fastidious nature. His trousers had been mouthed by that maidservant, and the thought revolted him. He rose and called for hot water to bathe.

The water was ready quickly. Song Zhang leaned against the edge of the bath, tilted his head back, and let a maidservant scrub him down.

Steam rose all around. He closed his eyes with a sigh of comfort.

But in the moment his eyes shut, the image that rose before him was Shen Weici's face — flushed with wine color, standing before Zhang Yuanheng with that faint, shy warmth — peach-pink at her cheeks like a breeze of spring had moved through.

He clenched his jaw and snapped his eyes open. He stared at the hot water lapping at his chest, and then the memory of that warmth between his fingers surfaced — Shen Weici's slight tilt of the head.

He was dazed for an instant. Then a heat rushed through him, and with a sharp, furious movement he shot to his feet from the bath.

He had no peace even soaking in a bath.

He was going right now to see what manner of creature this Shen Weici actually was. Or perhaps she had secretly used some trick on him too — bewitching him the same way she had apparently bewitched Zhang Yuanheng.

Water splashed loudly across the floor. The maidservant inside the bathing room was so startled she tumbled backward onto the floor, and when she raised her head again, the bathing room was empty.

Song Zhang called for servants to help him dress, left the sword behind, and walked out with a cold expression.

Minhe, standing guard at the door, saw Song Zhang walking out again, and quickly stepped forward: "Is the General heading to the Palace?"

"This one will go and have a carriage prepared."

Song Zhang's step paused. He looked at Minhe: "No need."

He opened his umbrella and walked into the curtain of rain.

The maidservants guarding the gate of Linchun Courtyard saw Song Zhang approaching from a distance and exchanged a startled, uncertain glance — they could not be sure he was really coming this way.

But the next moment he was in front of them — dark-robed, face dark as a death god — and they staggered back several steps in fright: "Second Young Master."

Song Zhang did not even glance at them. His clean, unhurried figure walked straight through into the inner room.

Yuedeng, sitting at the corridor tending the medicine brazier, saw Song Zhang coming straight toward her and nearly jumped out of her skin. She scrambled to her feet: "What brings Second Young Master here?"

Song Zhang stopped under the covered walkway and looked at her with sharp, clear eyes: "Where is your Third Miss?"

Yuedeng quickly said: "My young miss has only just fallen asleep. If Second Young Master has something to say, please tell me and I will pass it along when she wakes."

She had only just fallen asleep — it had been no time at all.

Song Zhang gave a cold laugh, stepped straight over the threshold, pushed through the bead curtain, rounded the screen, and walked inside.

He saw at once that Shen Weici was asleep on the daybed, her back to him. Her black hair was completely undone, spread across the pillows. One white arm lay over the quilt; her body was curled slightly inward.

Yuedeng came chasing after him, her face drained: "Second Young Master — my young miss's cold has not yet passed, and she drank fruit wine this afternoon. She has truly fallen asleep."

Song Zhang looked at Yuedeng with impatience: "You can either leave on your own, or have my man escort you out."

Yuedeng gaped at him: "Second Young Master — what exactly do you want with my young miss?"

Song Zhang had completely run out of patience. He said a single word, and Minhe, waiting outside, heard it and stepped wordlessly inside, pressed two fingers to the back of Yuedeng's neck, and caught her as she went limp. He carried her out.

Before leaving, Minhe swept a look around the room. It really was remarkably sparse. His general was barging in like this — it was actually rather unkind.

Though when he thought back, this was not actually the first time. He was fairly certain it was already several occasions.

In his experience, the General had never given any woman a second thought. If this counted as 'bullying,' it was unprecedented — to focus on one specific person like this.

Though Third Miss Shen did seem very gentle and easily pushed around.

But still...

Minhe decided not to think about it further. Carrying Yuedeng, he hurried out.

The room was left with only Song Zhang and Shen Weici. A hush fell over everything, broken only by the sound of rain from outside.

Song Zhang narrowed his eyes and looked around the room. He noticed the paper spread on the writing desk and walked over.

The characters written on the paper were neat and forceful — not what you would expect from a young woman. He glanced at the calligraphy copy lying beside it, picked it up, and looked at it — then let out a short, cold laugh.

He tossed the copy back onto the desk.

This was not something Shen Weici could possibly have come by herself. How it had come to her — he could work that out without much effort.

He walked over to the daybed. The person on it still had not moved. She looked truly asleep.

He bent to look, and what met his eyes was the vivid flush spread across Shen Weici's cheeks and her slightly parted, dark-red lips.

Those long lashes seemed to hold a trace of moisture, trembling almost imperceptibly.

Then from between those lips came two small, faint coughs. The coughs were barely audible, but the brows that had been softly parted furrowed — as though she too felt the discomfort, somewhere in her sleep.

Song Zhang paused, caught by the sight. Without quite deciding to, he leaned lower, wanting to see more clearly.

The elusive, gentle fragrance grew more present, but it was this same scent that suddenly brought him back to himself. He realized his face was less than a hand's span from Shen Weici's.

He could see, clearly, the pearl-soft luster of her ear, the fine dark strands of loose hair fanned across her cheek and shoulder, trailing into the opening of her collar.

From the curve of her neck to the slender waist, her body made an alluring silhouette, and the fingertips that fell from her sleeve trembled faintly.

Song Zhang had seen all manner of women. Women had knelt before him completely unclothed, and he had felt not the slightest stirring. Yet right now he was reacting to this glimpse of a small patch of collarbone — barely any skin at all.

He told himself she had bewitched him. Her scent was like some kind of aromatic catalyst — not heavy, not cloying, yet the moment he caught it, his gaze was drawn to her.

He drew his eyes back from the pale whiteness of her throat, and the coldness returned to them. He reached out and pinched Shen Weici's face, turning it toward him.

It was burning hot beneath his hand. He froze — and in that same moment, his none-too-gentle touch brought her awake. The foggy, hazy eyes opened, narrowed. The outer corners of her eyes were red.

Those eyes sharpened the moment they recognized who was in front of them: "Why are you here?"

Song Zhang looked at the expression in Shen Weici's eyes and gave a cold smile, releasing her face and then seizing her by the collar, pulling her toward him: "I go where I please. What say do you have in it?"

"Now — tell me what technique you've been using on Zhang Yuanheng, to have him coming to the Marquis estate every few days, fawning over you like this."

It had come to him now — the last time he had run into Zhang Yuanheng at the gate, the man had probably just left Shen Weici's company. No wonder — before, Zhang Yuanheng had never had any reason to call here. And then he suddenly appeared to 'discuss calligraphy.'

chapters.title: His Mind Full of Her
chapters.content:
Shen Weici found it utterly absurd — Song Zhang had burst into her room and was now demanding answers about something that had nothing whatsoever to do with him.

He was gripping her collar, the fabric bunched tight in his fist. Every time she tried to pull free, he only gripped harder. Her head was still swimming with the wine, still throbbing with a dull ache, and she looked up at him — her eyes reflecting the candlelight: "What business is it of yours?"

"More to the point — you entered my room without my permission. What gives you the right?"

"I may only have been in this household a short while, but I am the Third Miss the Old Madam acknowledged herself. That does not make me someone you can push around as you please."

"I would ask Song Young Master to have some regard for propriety."

His voice was pleasantly husky and grating all at once. Song Zhang's cold smile did not waver: "Propriety? I have underestimated you indeed — the schemes you run behind closed doors are hardly above board."

"Zhang Yuanheng refused two matchmakers just two months ago — yet somehow you managed to reel him in."

"I am simply curious what technique you used to drive a man out of his mind — made him brave this downpour to come deliver things to you."

"A woman like you, who climbs toward power and clings to the wealthy, is not necessarily someone the Zhang family will want."

Shen Weici would not suffer a single one of these outrageous words. She bit down her fury and met Song Zhang's mocking eyes with her own: "Whether I used a technique is not yours to say."

"Furthermore, what stands between Master Zhang and me is no business of yours. Whether the Zhang family wants me or not — also no business of yours."

"If Song Young Master entered my room today to call me to account — my conscience is clear. I would be perfectly willing to go before the Old Madam and let her judge the matter."

Song Zhang's eyes narrowed dangerously. His face went very dark. He stared at her flushed face, and his voice dropped lower: "I see you have a sharp tongue. Let me warn you — put away whatever arts you're practicing. Do not go around entangling men at will. If I catch you approaching Zhang Yuanheng again, don't blame me for showing you no mercy. I'll have you thrown out of this household."

Shen Weici felt only the hollowness of humiliation. Song Zhang's words made her eyes sting red — but she forced herself not to shed a single tear in front of this man.

She dug her fingers into her palm and endured the scalding shame, and asked him, fearlessly: "I only want to know — what does what exists between Master Zhang and me have to do with you?"

"You forced your way into my bedroom tonight. What rule gives you that right?"

These words landed somewhere in the very center of Song Zhang's being. Even now he could not fully account for what he had felt that afternoon — why the sight of what he had seen irritated him, made him restless, made him want to never see it again.

He found Shen Weici intolerable to look at. He did not want to see her sitting quietly in a corner somewhere, soft and warm as she spoke with someone, managing everything with effortless grace — all the while with those clear, cool eyes.

He was aware that the attention he paid to Shen Weici had grown excessive. Even now he could not stop himself from watching her face for any small change.

The feeling infuriated him — and the only release he could think of was to teach the person in front of him a lesson.

He was convinced she was some kind of enchantress. Otherwise, why would she occupy his thoughts like this? Otherwise, why would Zhang Yuanheng — of all people — be made into a lovesick fool before her?

He yanked her toward him by the collar, pulling her body forward, a cruel curve forming at the corner of his mouth: "What does it have to do with me? I simply cannot abide watching you ensnare men with your arts. You do not let a single one pass."

"What I've said — you had better remember. Carry on with these games, and this household will no longer be a place you are welcome to stay."

With that, Song Zhang released Shen Weici's collar with a rough shove. He looked at her — in a moon-white cross-collar single robe, falling back against the cushions, dark hair spreading out over her back.

She lay face-down against the pillow and did not move. She did not even make a sound. Song Zhang could only see scattered white amid the dark of her hair.

From the curve of her graceful back to the narrowing of her waist — then further, the subtle contour beneath hinting at something. Her fingertips hung from her sleeve, trembling faintly.

Song Zhang looked at that figure for a long time. Seductive and luminous all at once — like a bright moon caught in a spray of red blossoms.

Red tiles under white snow.

It made his heart fill with a scorching, rolling heat — and he felt almost a base, humbling impulse to surrender to it.

He did not feel the slightest satisfaction.

Enchantress.

Song Zhang looked at Shen Weici one last time. His tall, dark frame stirred the air as he turned, and he walked away with long, heavy strides.

He only felt a residual fire in him still, stirring those half-settled, impossible feelings. He had never wanted a woman so much.

Minhe, waiting outside, saw Song Zhang emerge with a black expression and quickly freed Yuedeng from the acupoint he had pressed and followed after him.

The rain outside had grown heavier. Song Zhang walked to the courtyard gate, then turned back abruptly to look at the window. The rain was loud and unceasing, but the room beyond it seemed as still and quiet as ever.

The oppression in his chest deepened. He raised his foot and walked away.

He did not go straight back to his own courtyard. He had a carriage prepared and went to his other residence in Wuyi Lane.

This house had been bestowed upon Song Zhang by the Emperor as a reward for distinguished service on the frontier — the lane housed only a few other families, all of them high-ranking officials and nobles.

Song Zhang rarely came here. Before, he had mostly returned to the Duke of Song's estate; it was only this past month he had been lingering longer in the Marquis household.

Guards were stationed in successive rings around the compound. Song Zhang pressed his lips tight and walked through the main courtyard, stepped over the threshold, then said in a low voice: "Find two women and bring them."

Minhe thought he had misheard. Was the General finally going to indulge himself?

In the past there had been no shortage of women around the General — but they were all ones who had thrust themselves forward, and the General had never deigned to touch any of them.

When the General had just come back to the capital from the frontier, after the Emperor placed the special guard on him, the fawning and the gifts of beautiful women had been considerable.

But ordinarily the General would not so much as glance at them — he gave every one of them straight to his subordinates.

A fair number of people outside had been saying the General was injured there and couldn't function. Even the Commandery Princess had been asking him privately.

Which was presumably why women kept being sent into the General's courtyard.

But at this moment — where was he supposed to find women on such short notice?

He hurried to find the head steward: "Didn't the Minister of Rites, Li, send the General several beautiful dancers a few days ago? Have you gotten rid of them?"

The steward shook his head: "They're still in the rear courtyard. The General hasn't been back in some time, and the General's subordinates wouldn't presume to move them."

Minhe was pleased: "Go and find two good-looking ones, clean and presentable, and have them wash up before attending to the General."

The steward was so startled he nearly thought he'd heard wrong. He had Minhe confirm it once more before he hurried off to make the selection.

Before long, inside the room, Song Zhang had untied the leather sash at his waist and sat on the edge of the bed, robe hanging half-open, long legs spread in that casual, unguarded posture he never showed elsewhere. Two women in gauze came gliding in through the door.

Both were exquisite, faces vivid and beautiful. The moment they entered and saw Song Zhang sitting there — those long legs encased in white trousers, the broad chest visible through the open robe, and that face — so handsome it should have been welcoming, yet with an expression of such cold indifference that it made the heart skip with something between fear and desire — they felt their cheeks grow hot.

They were not shy. From the moment they had been sent here, they had known what they were sent to do.

Both swayed forward, fingers sliding admiringly over Song Zhang's broad, solid arm — this arm, one of them thought privately, would do serious damage if it landed a punch; probably leave someone half-dead.

A thick, heavy perfume swept toward him. Song Zhang caught it and his brows knitted tighter, his face drawing more tense.

The two women noticed his expression and thought they must not be attending him properly. Their hands slid further, reaching for his collar to loosen it.

Song Zhang kept his eyes shut, trying to let that fire in him find an outlet. But behind his closed eyes all he could see was Shen Weici's wine-flushed face — those moist, peach-blossom eyes, and the sinuous curves beneath the white robe. The fire flared higher.

His jaw tightened, and he said through his teeth: "Enchantress."

He opened his eyes and looked at the two women in front of him — heavy makeup on painted faces. His hand closed into a fist. His voice fell cold and flat: "Get out."

The sound of it was frightening enough that both women, reading his expression, did not dare stay a moment longer. They stumbled and scrambled out the door.

Just then, Minhe slipped in and leaned close: "General — the Second Prince has come to call."

Song Zhang's brow furrowed. He sat still for a moment in thought, then straightened his collar and told someone to show the guest in.

chapters.title: Nothing but a Concubine-Born Daughter with No Backing
chapters.content:
Inside Linchun Courtyard, Yuedeng was helped to her feet by a maidservant. She glanced around in bewilderment for a moment, then quickly lifted the curtain and hurried into the inner room.

The inner room held only a single dim, yellow candle flame — cold and desolate. The sound of rain beat against the window paper, damp and chilling.

She found her young mistress lying face-down on the daybed, black hair spread across both shoulders, the thin blanket slipped down to her waist and hanging half off the edge, tracing the graceful curves of her body.

Though Shen Weici had not made a sound, Yuedeng's eyes were already red without her realizing it.

She suddenly remembered the night Lady Ling passed away — how Lady Ling had coughed blood onto Shen Weici's clothes and clung to her, reluctant to let go.

In the moment Lady Ling's eyes finally closed, Yuedeng had been kneeling at the bedside weeping until she nearly fainted. But Shen Weici had buried her face in Lady Ling's gradually cooling embrace and held her through the entire night, without uttering a single sound.

The next day, Shen Weici said: those who do evil will always pay a price — even the people closest to you.

Yuedeng walked softly to Shen Weici's side, bent down to pick up the thin blanket from the floor, and draped it over her, then called gently: "Miss."

But there was no reply even after a long while. Yuedeng pressed her hand to Shen Weici's back — ice cold.

Winter had set in by now, and rain made it even colder. The room had no charcoal fire, damp and freezing. Lying out in a single layer of clothing — most people could not have endured it.

She called again: "Miss, if you want to sleep, sleep on the proper bed. I'll also put in a warming brick for you."

"Supper will be here soon too — Miss needs to eat."

Only then did Shen Weici's cold, dangling fingers stir. She let the tears that had gathered in her eyes soak into the pillow, then pushed herself upright and sat.

Her black hair fell over both shoulders. She looked at Yuedeng and said in a hoarse voice: "Tell the maids outside not to breathe a word about Young Lord Song coming here just now."

Yuedeng saw Shen Weici's eyes were red-rimmed, her lashes still damp, and could not help sitting down beside her. She looked at Shen Weici's profile and said: "He was the one in the wrong to begin with — Miss didn't provoke him in any way. What was he doing, bullying you like that?"

"Even if Miss brought it before the Second Lord and the Old Madam, Miss would be in the right."

Shen Weici pressed her hand to her aching forehead and said quietly: "The match Father found for me — I don't want anything to go wrong with it. Every time Father has me go to the study to meet Master Zhang, I suspect the Second Lady still doesn't know about it."

"If I go to the Old Madam now, everyone in the Manor will find out."

"The Second Lady certainly doesn't want me marrying well — otherwise Father wouldn't have hidden it from her and told me not to mention it in front of her."

"The only thing that can put my mind at ease now is for Master Zhang to come and make his proposal soon."

Shen Weici rose and went to the proper bed, lay back down facing away from Yuedeng, and exhaled slowly: "Besides, Song Zhang belongs to the First Branch, holds a high position, and is not entirely a member of the Marquis Manor. Perhaps even the Old Madam has limited authority over him."

"And even if she tried, it would only be a case of deflecting with a light touch — and give others something to talk about besides."

"Yuedeng, have you forgotten what happened the time we played Shuanglu? Everyone saw clearly what happened, yet every one of them turned a blind eye. Even here in this Marquis Manor, everything comes down to whose interests are at stake."

"I am nothing but a concubine-born daughter with no backing. What does anyone lose by slighting me?"

"People weigh these things for themselves. I'm not going to humiliate myself by making a fuss."

Yuedeng was so distressed by these words that she went and crouched beside Shen Weici, murmuring: "Then what is to be done? Is Miss just supposed to endure being bullied by him?"

"If he barges in like this again for no reason, must she endure that too?"

Shen Weici turned to face Yuedeng, her eyes still damp, and covered Yuedeng's hand with her own cool fingers: "If he goes on insulting me without cause time after time, I naturally won't be able to endure it forever. Even if making a scene ends badly for me too, I would still tear away that false face of his — and let everyone in this Manor see it. For all their proud talk of noble standing, they single out only me to bully. Tell me — where is their dignity in that?"

Shen Weici said this, yet Yuedeng wavered: "But I'm afraid that if Miss offends Second Master Song, he'll retaliate even worse. They say he commands both Guard units and the Imperial Feathered Guard, controlling the palace army — and people say he has a ruthless heart. No one in the capital dares cross him."

"I can see that even the people in the Manor treat him with the utmost courtesy."

She looked at Shen Weici with uncertainty: "Perhaps Miss should just keep out of his way from now on. Once Master Zhang comes to propose, once the match is settled, Miss can leave the Manor."

Shen Weici looked at the earnest Yuedeng and lowered her lashes, a faint fragility beneath those dark brows: "Don't worry. I still have you by my side. I won't let things come to that unless I have no other choice."

She patted Yuedeng's hand: "Don't dwell on it. Yuedeng — I want to bathe."

Shen Weici's head was still throbbing, the wine unsettled in her body, leaving her in a dazed fog.

Yuedeng stared at Shen Weici's retreating figure for a moment, about to ask what exactly Second Master Song had come to say — but in the end said nothing, and silently withdrew to summon the maids.

Immersed in the bathing tub, the steam turned Shen Weici's cheeks a deeper shade of red. She rested her head on the tub's rim, her mind heavy with worry.

Her thoughts were clearer now. She turned Song Zhang's words over and over — baseless, incoherent rambling — and still could not fathom what he had come for.

Whatever there was between her and Zhang Yuanheng was not something that gave him any standing to interfere.

His accusation that she was seducing people — that arrogant look of his was nothing but contempt; in the marrow of his bones he believed himself superior to everyone, believed no gentleman would ever willingly marry her, and so he presumed whatever he liked.

Yet in revisiting the moment he had grabbed her by the collar, she could not help feeling the humiliation afresh. She blinked, and closed her eyes again.

When supper arrived, Shen Weici had no appetite at all.

She looked at the dishes already gone cold on the table, then turned her head toward the curtain, listening to the rain that had not let up. The wind set the curtain swaying, the gauze lifting and billowing; the lantern at the courtyard gate had long been blown out, and the far end of the small courtyard was pitch black — like a pair of eyes staring at her, malicious and unblinking.

Warning her to stay vigilant at every moment.

The silver chopsticks rested lightly on the small bowl. Shen Weici stood and walked to the corridor. The cold, damp wind carrying rain struck her face and swept away the last faint trace of color from her cheeks, leaving her complexion faintly pale again.

Strands of hair rose in the wind. The tree shadows lurched and grasped at the air. She looked at the water splashing beyond the corridor, at the weeds poking through cracks in the old flagstones, battered and scattered by the heavy rain — and something cold closed around her heart.

Yuedeng came out and draped a cloak over Shen Weici's shoulders: "What is there to look at in the rain? Miss's chill was almost gone — don't let it come back from the cold."

Shen Weici nodded, turned to look at Yuedeng, and gave a gentle smile: "You're right."

She drew the cloak tighter around herself, turned, and went back inside.

The room had been lit with several more candle flames. Shen Weici went and sat at the desk by the window, listening to the rain strike the window paper. She spread out a blank sheet before her, dipped her brush in ink, and began to write.

She wrote slowly, each character deliberate and precise. The candlelight stretched her slender, graceful silhouette long against the wall — the same softness, the same quiet weariness, as if carrying the faint trace of a fragrance.

chapters.title: Running Into Song Zhang Again
chapters.content:
The next morning, Shen Weici went to pay her respects to Lady Wen, who on this occasion issued a rare invitation for her to stay and share a meal.

It was a rest day, and Shen Rongshen was in as well. Lady Wen's invitation to join them for breakfast was likely a performance of goodwill put on for his benefit.

At the table, Shen Weici sat beside Shen Zhaozhao. As maids came and went, the breakfast table alone was laid with seven or eight dishes.

Shen Weici looked them over — most she had never tasted before. Braised white pork, pickled bamboo shoots, meat with yam — she lowered her eyes to the small bowl of shark's fin soup before her, something she had only ever heard of.

Her own courtyard usually received red date porridge or millet gruel, along with two plain vegetable dishes and one meat dish. Even that was more than she could finish. But here in the Second Branch's courtyard, it was far more lavish.

She had heard that the various branches could submit silver to the kitchen each month for better provisions. What was sent to her was presumably just the basic ration.

Once the dishes were set, Shen Rongshen lifted his chopsticks first. Shen Weici waited until the others had started, then reached for hers.

She also noticed the charcoal fire burning in the corner. She recalled that this room had begun burning charcoal much earlier in the season. She had asked around before and learned that the Manor distributed charcoal to the various courtyards after the onset of winter — but now it was well into winter, and her courtyard still had not received any.

No one spoke during the meal. After eating, they rinsed their mouths and washed their hands; maids brought towels and they dried themselves. By the time the whole routine was finished, the outside had grown fully bright.

Shen Rongshen smiled at Shen Zhaozhao: "You two sisters should spend more time together on ordinary days. Zhaozhao, take your Third Sister to your courtyard for a chat — after you're both married off someday, you should still keep in close touch."

Shen Zhaozhao had always looked down on Shen Weici, and her first instinct hearing her father's words was to refuse outright. But she remembered what her mother and grandmother had told her — if Shen Weici ended up married to Zhang Tingyi and bore a grudge against the family, it could cause real trouble. So she bit back her refusal.

Besides, she reasoned that with Shen Weici's cautious, quiet manner, she probably lacked the nerve for that anyway. Her mother and grandmother had reminded her several times, and she would just have to rein in her temper.

She turned to Shen Weici with a smile: "Would Third Sister like to come and sit in my courtyard for a while?"

Shen Weici looked at those ever-haughty eyes of Shen Zhaozhao's — eyes that had been pampered and indulged from childhood, polished to a golden arrogance, every emotion worn openly on her face. Did this sudden warm gesture today actually mean anything?

She pressed a handkerchief to her lips and coughed softly, then said in a quiet voice: "Last night on the way back the path was slippery, and I nearly fell — my umbrella even hit the ground, and I got a little wet. I think I've caught a chill. I'm afraid of passing it to Second Sister. Let me wait until I'm better, and I'll visit your courtyard another time."

Shen Zhaozhao had only asked out of appearances to begin with. She had nothing to say to Shen Weici — and at least the girl was sensible enough to make it easy.

Shen Rongshen, however, heard that Shen Weici was ill and stepped closer with a concerned word: "Is the chill serious? I'll have the Manor physician come see you later."

Shen Weici's gaze swept briefly over Lady Wen's expression, then looked back at Shen Rongshen and shook her head: "It's only a small cough — it will clear up in a day or two. Nothing to worry about."

Shen Rongshen nodded and added: "Your constitution is as delicate as your mother's. Don't let illness drag on. If it gets serious, remember to come and tell me."

Shen Weici answered obediently. In the instant she lowered her head, she caught from the corner of her eye the cool, knife-like gaze Lady Wen directed at her — as if it were carving a line across her face.

She said her farewells and went out.

Lady Wen's expression just now had been icy beyond words. The moment Shen Weici stepped outside, something cold lingered in her chest.

Barely had Shen Weici left than Lady Wen sent Shen Zhaozhao back to her own courtyard — and then promptly grabbed Shen Rongshen's ear and marched him into the inner room: "You — Shen Rongshen. So all these years you've never stopped thinking about that woman, have you?"

"I wondered why you were so attentive to that little — and now I see it's because you're still reminiscing about your old affair."

Shen Rongshen yelped as he was yanked inside, followed quickly by the sounds of his fawning and placating.

The maids in the courtyard were long past being surprised by such scenes. It never took long before the Second Lady would be sweetly charmed back into good spirits by the Second Lord.

By mid-morning, the Old Madam's senior maidservant came with a message. Shen Rongshen lifted the curtain and came out. He listened, then waved the girl away to relay an answer.

Lady Wen, who followed him out, asked: "What does the Old Madam want in the main hall at this hour?"

Shen Rongshen frowned: "What else could it be? The business about Xu Er, of course."

He gave a cold snort: "Making such a production of it — I know exactly what the Yong'an Marquis household is scheming. Wanting to bring pressure on the First Branch with numbers."

Lady Wen looked at him: "Xu Er is still sitting in the Feathered Guard's detention ward — who knows what the situation is, or what crime they're charging him with."

"Song Zhang is truly without any consideration for others. What could Xu Er possibly have done?"

"This is no small matter. If Xu Er is convicted, he is Zhi'an's own younger brother — what if it implicates Zhi'an? And even if nothing happens to Zhi'an, Zhaozhao is to marry him next year. Won't his family have something to say? Won't there be friction between husband and wife from the start?"

"Getting Xu Er released would be better for Zhaozhao too."

Shen Rongshen said coldly: "Xu Er is a good-for-nothing — and that's entirely his father and brother's doing, spoiling him to no end. He was bound to cause trouble sooner or later."

He said it, but still had someone sent to summon both Shen Zhaozhao and Shen Weici.

At that moment, Shen Weici had just asked Yuedeng to go inquire with the housekeeper about the charcoal. Yuedeng had only just returned, had not yet managed to speak, when the summons arrived — just saying the Second Lord was calling her to the main hall, with no explanation, and was gone.

Shen Weici told Yuedeng they would speak later, tidied herself briefly, and brought Yuedeng along to the main hall.

When she arrived, she found all three branches present, with the sole exception of Princess Consort Huimin, who was, as always, absorbed in her Buddhist devotions and took no part in worldly affairs.

Shen Zhaozhao and Shen Yanli were already seated on one side. On the other side of the main hall stood a figure — upright and handsome, a young man she did not recognize, speaking to the Old Madam.

She did not look at him at length. She offered her greetings to the Old Madam and the lords and ladies of the Third Branch, then found herself a seat in a corner and sat down.

No sooner had she sat than she felt a gaze settle on her. She looked up — and met the eyes of Song Zhang, seated directly across from her.

He wore his usual dark-colored robe threaded with gold, his hair bound with a gold crown, his whole bearing shadowed and cold. His long, narrow phoenix eyes, as if sensing her glance, swept lazily over toward her.

Their eyes met. Shen Weici gave a slight start, then looked away and lowered her head to drink her tea, treating him as though she had never seen him at all.

On his side, Song Zhang watched Shen Weici look away from him — as if she had spotted something unpleasant — and his eyes narrowed.

It was only when the First Lord nudged his arm that he returned his attention to the young man standing in the hall: Xu Zhi'an.

chapters.title: A White Fox-Fur Collar
chapters.content:
Song Zhang lounged against the back of his chair, sitting with scandalous ease beside the First Lord, one long leg propped over the other. His slender fingers drummed impatiently on the armrest as he regarded Xu Zhi'an with indifferent coldness, his voice drawling and low: "The Yong'an Marquis household has quite the nerve. Paying a visit to the Manor and expecting the entire household to turn out and receive you — truly an eye-opening experience."

Xu Zhi'an hurried to clasp his hands toward Song Zhang from the center of the hall: "General Song misunderstands. The reason I asked everyone to gather is that two months ago, my younger brother shot several white foxes while out on the autumn hunt. With winter upon us, I had them made into fur collars to present to the young ladies of the household — which is why I took the liberty of inviting everyone together."

"I've also had some red fox-fur knee warmers made for the young gentlemen of the household, all as a small token of goodwill."

He then turned to clasp his hands toward the Old Madam and bow: "I've come without much notice — please don't take it amiss, Old Madam Shen."

He bowed in turn to everyone else seated in the hall, his manner humble and courteous: "I've imposed on all of you — I hope none of you will find fault."

Every courtesy was observed, nothing to criticize.

He then produced a box and presented it before Old Madam Shen: "This is a whole red fox skin my younger brother shot last year on Pine Mountain — the fur is lustrous and soft. It's a special gift brought especially for the Old Madam's comfort."

The Old Madam glanced at the box before her, then at Song Zhang. She understood perfectly well what this visit was about.

One could hardly refuse a gift brought in person — but to accept was to make accommodations.

She turned it over briefly in her mind and then smiled and accepted it.

After all, the two households were to be united by marriage. There would be ongoing dealings between them, and it was better to help where one could.

Seeing the Old Madam accept, Xu Zhi'an felt his heart lighten, and he had his attendants bring out the boxes one by one, personally presenting one to each of the young ladies of the Manor.

Shen Weici received one as well. She raised her head and saw a pair of slender, refined fingers before her. She had just taken it when she heard a voice: "I'm afraid I don't know this young lady?"

The Old Madam smiled at that: "She was frail from childhood and was raised at an estate outside the city. She's only just been brought back."

She added with a light laugh: "She is also of the Second Branch — a few months younger than Zhaozhao. You really ought to get acquainted."

Xu Zhi'an looked at Shen Weici with genuine attention — skin like flawless jade, her bearing moving and lovely. Among the Manor's young ladies, she stood out with particular vividness, and he looked again, quietly, a second and third time.

"Indeed I should," he said with a smile.

Shen Zhaozhao noticed Xu Zhi'an's gaze lingering on Shen Weici and was immediately displeased. She was by nature straightforward, and Xu Zhi'an was her intended — why should he be getting acquainted with Shen Weici, this illegitimate daughter of dubious standing?

She spoke her mind at once: "And what has Xu Brother prepared especially for me?"

At the sound of Shen Zhaozhao's voice, Xu Zhi'an went to her side with an indulgent smile: "What I prepared for you, naturally, is different from the rest."

Song Zhang looked at Xu Zhi'an's performance of a proper gentleman and found it frankly ridiculous. He didn't know how many serving maids the man kept warm in his bed, how many scenes of jealousy and rivalry that had caused — yet he managed to put on such a respectable face outside.

He did not spare feelings as he sneered: "Can Xu Qing's archery actually hit a fox?"

"He's soaking in women all day — I'd wager he hasn't the strength left for it. I doubt he could even lift a bow at this point."

"And a few white fox-fur collars — what's so remarkable about that? My trained heron goes out and can bring one back in its beak for me. I wouldn't even glance at it — I hand them off to my men."

Xu Zhi'an paused. He knew Song Zhang's temperament well: he showed no one face.

He kept his smile in place and looked at Song Zhang: "It is nothing but a token of goodwill — value is hardly the measure."

Song Zhang met Xu Zhi'an's smile with a deep, settling look: "Oh? Goodwill? If you truly had any goodwill, you would have kept your own brother under control."

Xu Zhi'an's expression stiffened. Song Zhang was speaking this way in front of the entire assembled household without so much as a thought for appearances.

He had expected Song Zhang to show at least some regard for the Old Madam's presence and for the Second Branch's dignity. But apparently he did not intend to spare even the Old Madam's face.

Shen Zhaozhao was also rigid with discomfort. Xu Zhi'an was her intended — to have him openly humiliated by Song Zhang in front of all these people was as much a slap to her own face.

She sat as if on pins and needles, her expression carefully unhappy as she looked at Song Zhang.

But Song Zhang did not spare her a single glance, and her face went alternately pale and flushed.

Shen Rongshen also felt that Song Zhang had gone too far. Even if he privately understood why Xu Zhi'an had come with gifts, the man had at least shown sincerity and made a gesture of goodwill. Song Zhang was effectively half a member of the Marquis Manor household — this was not how to behave.

He looked at Song Zhang and said: "Zhi'an comes with a good heart. I quite like this fur collar myself — it's not a trifle. White fox is already rare. That he's thought to bring some for the Manor's young ladies speaks to genuine consideration."

Song Zhang rose to his feet with languid indifference: "Goodwill is something I can't be bothered to appreciate. Nor do I have the patience to sit here watching this sort of charade. An entirely wasted trip."

He said this and made to leave.

It was only now that the First Lord, who had said nothing all along, finally opened his mouth. He glanced at Song Zhang and said quietly: "Sit down, Zhanger."

Of all the people in this Manor, the only one Song Zhang could manage to hold in any real respect was this stepfather of his. He paused, cast the First Lord a look, let his gaze slide past Shen Weici, and sat back down.

Shen Shen, seeing Song Zhang seated, glanced at the Yong'an Marquis across from him — who had yet to say a word — and leaned back in his chair, saying evenly: "Marquis Xu, there's no need to say it sideways. You could have come and spoken plainly with me. There was no need to summon the whole household."

The Yong'an Marquis, who had been sitting there stiffly, had not expected Song Zhang to be this blatant. Though he himself was no longer in office, his son had done rather well — passed the jinshi examination — and Song Zhang was nothing but an imperial relative by blood, treating everyone as beneath him.

The man wielded the sword the Emperor had given him and had served as the Emperor's vanguard on any number of occasions these past two years. The Marquis knew perfectly well that no one in the capital dared cross Song Zhang.

He also knew he was no match for him — let alone that the Song Ducal Manor's old Duke still commanded troops, making the Song family far more powerful than his own.

What frightened him most was the possibility that the Emperor might move against his household, or that his son had been associating with the wrong people outside, saying things he should not have — which could implicate the entire family.

Moreover, he had sent his daughter to beg the Emperor for clemency, and the Emperor had said the matter was entirely for Song Zhang to decide. That alone showed Song Zhang's standing with the Emperor.

With the crown prince still unestablished and the court's political alignments unclear, he dared not take sides lightly.

He swallowed his frustration and addressed Shen Shen: "Marquis Shen, we came today in a spirit of courtesy and goodwill. General Song may have no regard for the gift — but it was a gesture of sincerity, was it not?"

"The Yong'an Marquis household and the Jian'an Marquis household are joined by a marriage alliance. After next year, when Zhi'an formally weds Second Young Miss Shen, we will all be family — mutual care and support is only natural."

"My worthless, reckless son — I know him. He had too much wine and said some foolish things. He didn't mean any of it, and had no real audacity behind his words."

"I have come today for my Second Boy. But I ask Marquis Shen to show some consideration for the sake of family ties."

He then looked toward Shen Rongshen: "And I ask my good in-law to put in a word of intercession on my Second Boy's behalf."

The Marquis rose as he spoke, bowing with clasped hands to both Shen Shen and Shen Rongshen.

Shen Rongshen looked uncomfortable at having the matter put this plainly and glanced at his elder brother.

Shen Shen sat back and considered. He did not particularly care about the Yong'an Marquis — but his younger brother's situation still needed some looking after. He looked at Song Zhang: "What crime has Xu Er committed?"

Song Zhang turned his teacup idly in his hands: "Send him to the Court of Judicial Review tomorrow and you'll find out."

The Yong'an Marquis's face changed. He looked at Song Zhang and said in a measured voice: "General Song, show some mercy where you can. We will certainly come again to express our gratitude."

Song Zhang glanced at the Marquis bowing before him, stroked his chin, and then looked toward the corner where Shen Weici sat — head slightly lowered, seeming utterly removed from the whole scene.

He had been in a foul mood since last night, and it was only fair that she share some of his displeasure.

She had the nerve to avoid his gaze — well, then let everyone's eyes fall on her.

He opened his mouth: "Releasing Xu Er isn't impossible. In that case, let Third Young Miss Shen play a game of Shuanglu with me. If Third Young Miss can beat me, I'll release Xu Er."

Song Zhang let a faint smile curve his lips, and met the look of astonishment that Shen Weici turned on him.

chapters.title: Playing Chess Against Song Zhang
chapters.content:
A momentary hush fell over the main hall. No one had expected Song Zhang to put forward such a demand.

It was like something out of a game.

Shen Shen frowned at Song Zhang: "Zhanger, a matter like this — this is no way to handle it."

Song Zhang looked at Shen Shen: "Arresting Xu Qing was not a game either. The Yong'an Marquis household brings gifts and expects me to release him — is that not a game?"

He stood and smoothed his robe: "If it is indeed a game, then let it go."

He took a few steps toward the door — only to be blocked by Xu Zhi'an: "General Song, did you mean that? That if she wins, you'll release my brother?"

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow, a thread of impatience in his cool eyes: "Do you think I'm joking with you?"

Xu Zhi'an's face stiffened. He turned and asked Shen Weici: "May I ask whether Third Young Miss Shen knows how to play Shuanglu?"

Shen Weici had not expected Song Zhang to direct everyone's attention toward her. If she failed to win, the blame would fall on her shoulders.

She looked past Song Zhang and addressed her father quietly: "Father, I know only the basics of Shuanglu — I wouldn't dare play against Young Lord Song."

Shen Rongshen also frowned. Shen Weici had grown up in a small town — she was unlikely to be skilled at Shuanglu. He turned to Song Zhang to negotiate: "Couldn't we change the opponent?"

"Perhaps Zhaozhao could play with you instead."

Song Zhang glanced at Shen Weici's slightly bowed head with flat indifference: "If we're changing people, then forget it. I don't have time to waste here."

Even with only a slim chance, it was worth trying. Xu Zhi'an quickly said to Shen Weici: "Third Young Miss, please just play — if you lose, no one will blame you."

Shen Zhaozhao's eyes fixed on Shen Weici's face, baffled as to why the Young Lord would want to play Shen Weici. Should he not be playing her?

At this point the Old Madam spoke as well, addressing Shen Weici: "Since Song Zhang has named you, go."

Every gaze in the room turned to her at once, and now the Old Madam had also spoken. Shen Weici lowered her lashes, refusing to look at Song Zhang's eyes on her, and quietly agreed.

A servant quickly brought a game board over. Shen Weici and Song Zhang sat facing each other. She looked at him and found him looking back.

She said nothing and waited for the maid beside them to draw lots for who would go first.

The draw fell to Shen Weici. Shen Zhaozhao at her side immediately urged: "Go on, make your move."

Shen Weici was quiet. She began to shake the dice, then moved her piece according to her usual habit.
